newsitem.title: USA: Big pension funds attack ADM board makeup.
newsitem.headline: Big pension funds attack ADM board makeup.

text.p: Two major pension funds are firing another salvo in their campaign for a resolution to put more independent directors on troubled agribusiness giant Archer Daniel Midlands Co.'s board.

The California Public Employees' Retirement System (Calpers) and the Florida Retirement System Trust Fund are urging ADM shareholders to support a proposal to change the company's bylaws to require a board majority be composed of independent directors.

"We intend to pursue our shareholder resolution vigorously," Calpers Chief Executive Jim Burton said Tuesday in Frankfurt, Germany. "We are unhappy with the make-up of the board. We don't believe that they are following the intents of their own governance committee."
Burton, in Europe to promote investment in California, said he was slated to meet with ADM Monday, ahead of the Decatur, Ill.-based company's annual meeting Oct. 17.
The proposal by Calpers and the Florida trust fund is among three shareholder proposals that address corporate governance issues at ADM, which is the focus of a federal antitrust probe.
The Justice Department is investigating alleged price fixing for lysine, a feed additive; citric acid, a food additive, and high-fructose corn syrup, a sweetener commonly used in beverages.

ADM has said indictments are being considered in the lysine probe against it and two top executives -- Michael Andreas, vice chairman and son of Chairman Dwayne Andreas, and Terrance Wilson, vice president in charge of corn refining operations.

Also on the ADM proxy is a proposal by the United Brotherhood of Carpenters Pension Fund to hold company directors liable for monetary damages in cases of gross negligence. The New York City Fire Department Pension Fund also put forward a proposal, for confidential voting for directors when there is no competing proxy.
Institutional shareholders raised the issue of corporate governance and the independence of board members at ADM after the company became the target of a federal probe.
In a statement, Calpers and the Florida fund said ADM's board "fails to meet even a watered-down version of independence."

"When outside directors who are also relatives, customers, suppliers and friends are asked to judge performance of the company and its management -- how 'independent' will they be?" the statement said.
Amid the price-fixing probe, several lawsuits have been filed against ADM by customers, alleging they paid inflated prices for lysine, citric acid and high-fructose corn syrup.

Earlier this year, ADM agreed to pay $25 million to settle a lawsuit by lysine customers. Last week, it agreed to pay $35 million to settle a lawsuit by citric acid customers. It also agreed last week to pay $30 million to settle a securities lawsuit by a group of shareholders. ADM did not admit to violating the law in any of the settlements.
However, the company still faces potentially the costliest lawsuit brought by buyers of the corn syrup, plaintiffs' attorneys said.
Attorneys representing a class of about 2,700 plaintiffs said no settlement is expected soon in the corn syrup lawsuit brought against ADM on grounds of alleged price fixing.
"There's nothing on the horizon right now," said Laddie Montague, one of three co-lead counsels for the plaintiffs.
The litigation is the last -- and potentially the biggest -- case brought against ADM by its customers, Montague said.
Attorneys said the plaintiffs, including food and beverage companies, are seeking treble damages for allegedly paying inflated prices. The total amount of damages being sought was not disclosed.
Soft drink giants Coca-Cola Co. and PepsiCo Inc. are among the plaintiffs, Montague said.
A trial date has been set for March 1998.
